claim: Disclosure norms for AI in applications are themselves unsettled and moving: Caltech briefly used a confidential self-disclosure question ('Did you receive any AI generated assistance') for Fall 2025, then replaced it for Fall 2026 with a mandatory guidelines-review-plus-rescission model and no standalone disclosure prompt. No major school requires applicants to disclose PERMITTED uses (grammar, brainstorming). The practical norm in 2024-2026 is therefore: schools that address AI ask for attestation of authorship, not an itemized AI-use log -- and the small number that experimented with explicit disclosure have not converged.

application.content: Advise students NOT to volunteer a list of AI uses unless a school's application explicitly asks (it almost never does in 2026). Over-disclosing permitted use (e.g. 'I used Grammarly') adds nothing and can read as defensiveness; the operative obligation is the authorship attestation. The ONE exception: if a specific school's application contains an AI-use question that cycle, answer it honestly and completely -- a false 'no' there is its own integrity violation, separate from the essay content.

provenanceTrail: Two Caltech cycle-specific URLs (Fall 2025 and Fall-2026 'first-year-applicants') both surfaced in search 2026-06-18; the existence of a distinct Fall-2025 page plus a current page with different mechanics establishes the year-over-year change. The dropping of the explicit confidential disclosure question was corroborated by a 2026 secondary roundup. Caltech is the clearest documented case of disclosure-norm flux; entry deliberately scoped to disclosure to avoid overclaiming a stable industry norm where none exists.
